content.narrative_summary: This section introduces the purpose and scope of the ESC Guidelines, emphasizing evidence-based recommendations for diagnostic and therapeutic approaches. content.narrative_summary: Figure 1 presents a central illustration of a holistic, multidisciplinary approach to peripheral arterial and aortic diseases across the continuum of care. The cycle includes Prevention (awareness, CVRF management, screening, genetic counselling), Diagnosis (clinical, functional, QoL assessment, imaging), Treatment (medical therapy, education, CVRF control, rehabilitation, intervention consideration), and Follow-up (regular review, tailored targets, family screening). Surrounding the cycle are key team members: cardiologist, cardiac surgeon, CV radiologist, CV intensive care specialist, anaesthetist, nephrologist, nurse, neurologist, exercise therapist, geneticist, vascular surgeon, and angiologist. Below, Goals (prevent atherosclerosis, improve QoL, reduce MACE/MALE, hospitalization, interventions) and Initial steps (PAAD risk screening, early access, optimal treatment) are highlighted.

content.narrative_summary: Multiple recommendation tables covering antithrombotic therapy, interventional and medical treatment strategies, follow-up protocols, and diagnostic assessments in peripheral arterial disease, chronic limb-threatening ischaemia, carotid and subclavian stenosis, and renal artery disease.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for antithrombotic therapy in patients with peripheral arterial disease

rows.recommendation: Treatment with combination rivaroxaban (2.5 mg b.i.d.) and aspirin (100 mg o.d.) should be considered for patients with PAD and high ischaemic risk, and non-high bleeding risk.
Treatment with combination rivaroxaban (2.5 mg b.i.d.) and aspirin (100 mg o.d.) should be considered for patients with PAD and non-high bleeding risk following lower-limb revascularization.
Aspirin (75–100 mg) for primary prevention may be considered in patients with asymptomatic PAD and DM, in the absence of contraindications.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for interventional treatment of asymptomatic and symptomatic peripheral arterial disease (general)

rows.recommendation: In patients with symptomatic PAD, after a 3 month period of OMT and exercise therapy, PAD-related QoL assessment is recommended.
It is recommended to adapt the mode and type of revascularization options to anatomical lesion location, lesion morphology, and general patient condition.
In patients with symptomatic PAD and impaired PAD-related QoL after a 3 month period of OMT and exercise therapy, revascularization may be considered.
In patients with PAD, revascularization is not recommended if the reason is to solely prevent progression to CLTI.
In patients with asymptomatic PAD, revascularization is not recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for interventional treatment of patients with symptomatic peripheral arterial disease (per arterial bed)

rows.recommendation: In femoro-popliteal lesions, drug-eluting treatment should be considered as the first-choice strategy.
In femoro-popliteal lesions, if revascularization is indicated, an open surgical approach should be considered when an autologous vein (e.g. GSV) is available in patients with low surgical risk.
In patients with severe IC undergoing endovascular femoro-popliteal revascularization, treatment of BTK arteries may be considered in the same intervention.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations in patients with peripheral arterial disease: follow-up of patients with peripheral arterial disease

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to regularly, at least once a year, follow-up patients with PAD, assessing clinical and functional status, medication adherence, limb symptoms, and CVRFs, with DUS assessment as needed.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of chronic limb-threatening ischaemia

rows.recommendation: Early recognition of CLTI and referral to the vascular team are recommended for limb salvage.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for medical treatment in patients with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that patients with CLTI are managed by a vascular team.
In patients with CLTI and ulcers, offloading mechanical tissue stress is indicated to allow wound healing.
Lower-limb exercise training is not recommended in patients with CLTI and wounds.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for interventional treatment of chronic limb-threatening ischaemia

rows.recommendation: In CLTI patients, it is recommended to perform revascularization as soon as possible.
In CLTI, it is recommended to use autologous veins as the preferred conduit for infra-inguinal bypass surgery.
In multilevel vascular disease, it is recommended to eliminate inflow obstructions when treating downstream lesions.
In CLTI patients with good autologous veins and low surgical risk (<5% peri-operative mortality, >50% 2 year survival), infra-inguinal bypass may be considered.
In CLTI patients, endovascular treatment may be considered as first-line therapy, especially in patients with increased surgical risk or inadequate autologous veins.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for follow-up in patients with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia

rows.recommendation: In patients with CLTI, following revascularization it is recommended to follow-up patients on a regular basis.
At follow-up, it is recommended to assess clinical, haemodynamic and functional status, limb symptoms, treatment adherence, and CVRFs.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for carotid artery stenosis assessment

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to use the NASCET method or its non-invasive equivalent to assess ICA stenosis.
It is not recommended to use the ECST method for ICA stenosis assessment.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of subclavian artery stenosis

rows.recommendation: Bilateral arm BP measurement is recommended for all patients with PAAD.
Endovascular revascularization may be considered over surgery, despite similar long-term outcomes, due to lower complication rates.
Routine revascularization in patients with atherosclerotic subclavian artery disease is not recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for diagnostic strategies for renal artery disease

rows.recommendation: DUS is recommended as the first-line imaging modality in patients with suspicion of RAS.

content.narrative_summary: Multiple recommendation tables covering treatment strategies for renal and visceral artery disease, surgical criteria for aortic root, ascending aorta and arch aneurysms, follow-up protocols after aneurysm repair, diagnostic work-up and medical management of acute aortic syndromes, and interventions in type A acute aortic dissection.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for treatment strategies for renal artery disease: Revascularization

rows.recommendation: In patients with atherosclerotic unilateral >70% RAS, concomitant high-risk features, and signs of kidney viability, renal artery revascularization should be considered after OMT has been established.
In patients with atherosclerotic bilateral (>70%) RAS or RAS in a solitary kidney, concomitant high risk features, and signs of kidney viability, renal artery revascularization should be considered.

In patients with hypertension and/or signs of renal dysfunction due to RAS caused by fibromuscular dysplasia, concomitant high-risk features, and signs of kidney viability, revascularization with primary balloon angioplasty and bailout stenting should be considered.
In patients with an indication for renal artery revascularization and complex anatomy, or after failed endovascular revascularization, open surgical revascularization should be considered.
In patients with atherosclerotic unilateral RAS, routine revascularization is not recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations in patients with visceral artery stenosis

rows.recommendation: In patients with acute or chronic mesenteric ischaemia, assessment by a vascular team is recommended.
Revascularization of asymptomatic atherosclerotic visceral artery stenosis is not recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for surgery in aortic root and ascending aorta dilatation associated with tricuspid aortic valve

rows.recommendation: In patients with dilatation of the tubular ascending aorta who can be offered surgery with low predicted risk, ascending aortic replacement should be considered at a maximum diameter >52 mm.

In patients undergoing surgery for tricuspid aortic valve disease who have concomitant dilatation of the aortic root or ascending tubular aorta, and low predicted surgical risk, ascending aorta or root replacement should be considered at a maximum diameter ≥45 mm, otherwise >50 mm.
SAPT with low-dose aspirin (75–100 mg/day) should be considered for the first 3 months after valve-sparing aortic surgery when there are no other baseline indications for OAC.

In patients undergoing non-aortic-valve cardiac surgery who have concomitant dilatation of the ascending aorta or aortic root with a maximum diameter ≥50 mm, concomitant aortic surgery should be considered.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for surgery in aortic arch aneurysms

rows.recommendation: In patients with low or intermediate operative risk with an aortic arch aneurysm and recurrent episodes of chest pain not attributable to non-aortic causes, open surgical replacement of the arch is recommended.

In patients undergoing open surgical repair of an aortic arch aneurysm, an elephant trunk or frozen elephant trunk procedure should be considered if the aneurysmal disease extends into the proximal descending thoracic aorta.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for follow-up after treatment of aortic aneurysms

rows.recommendation: After open repair of TAA, an early CCT is recommended within 1 month, and then yearly CCT follow-up for the first 2 post-operative years and every 5 years thereafter is recommended if findings are stable.
After 5 post-operative years without complications, continuing long-term follow-up of TEVAR by CCT every 5 years should be considered.
If growth of the excluded aneurysm is observed, without evidence of type I or II endoleak, repeating CCT every 6–12 months, depending on the growth rate observed, should be considered.
In low-risk patients, from 1 year post-operatively after EVAR, repeating DUS/CEUS every 2 years should be considered.
If any abnormality during DUS/CEUS is found, confirmation should be considered with additional CCT or CMR (based on potential artefacts).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for diagnostic work-up of acute aortic syndrome

rows.recommendation: CCT from neck to pelvis is recommended as the first-line imaging technique in patients with suspected AAS since it is widely available, accurate, and provides information about the entry tear, extension, and possible complications (malperfusion, dilatation, or rupture).
In patients with suspected AAS, TOE is recommended to guide peri-operative management and detect complications.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for medical treatment in acute aortic syndromes

rows.recommendation: In patients with AAS who can be managed conservatively and who achieved haemodynamic targets with i.v. anti-impulse therapy, switching to oral BBs and, if necessary, up-titration of other BP-lowering agents is recommended after 24 h if gastrointestinal transit is preserved.
If the patient has a contraindication for BBs, a non-dihydropyridine calcium blocker should be considered.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for intervention in type A acute aortic dissection

rows.recommendation: In patients with acute TAAD who have extensive destruction of the aortic root, a root aneurysm, or a known genetic aortic disorder, aortic root replacement is recommended with a mechanical or biological valved conduit.

In patients presenting with acute TAAD, transfer from a low- to a high-volume aortic centre with the presence of a multidisciplinary team should be considered to improve survival if transfer can be accomplished without significant delay in surgery.
In selected patients, a valve-sparing root repair may be considered, when performed by experienced surgeons.

content.narrative_summary: This page presents a series of structured recommendations across multiple aspects of aortic disease management, including surgical repair strategies for type A dissection, malperfusion management, acute and chronic type B dissection interventions, penetrating ulcer treatment, traumatic aortic injury repair, follow-up imaging protocols after acute aortic syndrome, management of heritable thoracic aortic disease, and consideration of genetic testing and aortic screening guided by underlying gene/variant.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for aortic repair strategies in type A acute aortic dissection

rows.recommendation: In patients with acute TAAD and a partially dissected aortic root but no significant aortic valve leaflet pathology, aortic valve resuspension is recommended over valve replacement.
In patients with acute TAAD undergoing aortic repair, an open distal anastomosis is recommended to improve survival and increase FL thrombosis rates.
In patients with acute TAAD without an intimal tear in the arch or a significant arch aneurysm, hemi-arch repair is recommended over more extensive arch replacement.

In patients with acute TAAD and a secondary intimal tear in the arch or proximal DTA, extended aortic repair with stenting of the proximal DTA (e.g. by the frozen elephant technique) may be considered to reduce late distal aortic complications (e.g. aneurysm evolution of the remaining dissected descending aorta).

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of malperfusion in the setting of acute aortic dissection

rows.recommendation: In patients with acute TAAD presenting with malperfusion (cerebral, mesenteric, lower limb, or renal), immediate aortic surgery is recommended.
In patients with acute TAAD presenting with cerebral malperfusion or non-haemorrhagic stroke, immediate aortic surgery should be considered to improve neurological outcome and reduce mortality.

In patients with acute TAAD presenting with clinically significant mesenteric malperfusion syndrome, immediate invasive angiographic diagnostics to evaluate percutaneous malperfusion repair before or directly after aortic surgery, in aortic centres with expertise, should be considered.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of patients presenting with acute type B aortic dissection

rows.recommendation: In patients with uncomplicated acute TBAD, TEVAR in the subacute phase (between 14 and 90 days) should be considered in selected patients with high-risk features to prevent aortic complications.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of patients presenting with chronic type B aortic dissection

rows.recommendation: In chronic TBAD and with a descending thoracic aortic diameter ≥60 mm, treatment is recommended in patients at reasonable surgical risk.
In patients with chronic TBAD and a descending thoracic aortic diameter ≥55 mm, an indication for intervention should be considered in patients with low procedural risk.
In patients with chronic post-dissection thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysms, the use of fenestrated/branched stent grafts may be considered, when treatment is indicated.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer

rows.recommendation: In uncomplicated type B PAU with high-risk imaging features, endovascular treatment should be considered.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for traumatic aortic injury

rows.recommendation: In cases of severe aortic injury (grade 4), immediate repair is recommended.
In minimal aortic injury (grades 1 or 2), initial medical therapy under careful clinical and imaging surveillance should be considered.
In cases of progression of the IMH (grade 2), semi-selective repair (within 24–72 h) should be considered.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for follow-up after treatment of acute aortic syndrome

rows.recommendation: In medically treated type B AAS or IMH, follow-up imaging is recommended at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months after onset, then yearly if imaging findings are stable.
In medically treated PAU, follow-up imaging is recommended at 1 month after diagnosis, then every 6 months if imaging findings are stable.
After open surgery for AAS, follow-up imaging by CCT and TTE within 6 months, then CCT at 12 months and then yearly if findings are stable, should be considered.
If no complications occur within the first 5 years, CCT every 2 years thereafter should be considered.
If no residual patent FL is documented for 3 post-operative years, subsequent surveillance by CCT every 2–3 years should be considered.
In the follow-up of medically treated PAU, after 2 years of imaging stability, larger intervals should be considered in low-risk patients.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of patients with heritable thoracic aortic disease

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that medical management of patients with HTAD is individualized and based on shared decision-making.
It is recommended that patients with known or suspected syndromic or non-syndromic HTAD are evaluated in a centre with experience in the care of this patient group.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for genetic testing and aortic screening in aortic disease

rows.recommendation: In patients with HTAD, guidance of clinical management by the underlying gene/variant, when known, should be considered.

content.narrative_summary: This page presents guideline recommendations for imaging, surgical intervention, medical therapy, pregnancy management, and exercise in patients with Turner syndrome, vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, Loeys–Dietz syndrome, and ACTA2-related heritable thoracic aortic disease. Each section lists specific indications, modalities, surveillance intervals, and treatment considerations with corresponding class of recommendation and level of evidence.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for imaging in women with Turner syndrome

rows.recommendation: To take the smaller body size of women (≥15 years) with TS into account, the use of the ascending ASI (ratio of aortic diameter [mm] to BSA [m²]), AHI (ratio of aortic diameter [mm] to height [m]), or aortic z-score is recommended to define the degree of aortic dilatation and assess the risk of aortic dissection.
It is recommended to define imaging and clinical surveillance intervals according to the estimated risk for dissection, based on the ascending ASI and concomitant lesions.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for aortic surgery in women with Turner syndrome

rows.recommendation: In patients with vEDS, regular vascular surveillance of the aorta and peripheral arteries by DUS, CCT, or CMR is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for vascular imaging in Marfan syndrome

rows.recommendation:

• At least every 6 months in patients with an aortic root diameter <45 mm in the presence of additional risk factors
• At least every 6–12 months in patients with an aortic root diameter ≥45 mm in the absence of additional risk factors

In patients without previous aortic surgery, complete peripheral vascular and thoracoabdominal aortic imaging by CMR or CCT and DUS is recommended at the first evaluation, and subsequently every 3–5 years if stable.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for medical treatment in Marfan syndrome

rows.recommendation: In patients with MFS, treatment with either a BB or an ARB, in maximally tolerated doses (unless contraindicated), is recommended to reduce the rate of aortic dilatation.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for pregnancy in women with Marfan syndrome

rows.recommendation:

• Have follow-up in a centre with access to a pregnancy heart and vessel team
It is recommended that couples in which a partner has or is at risk of HTAD be offered pre-conception genetic counselling.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for physical exercise in patients with Marfan syndrome

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to individualize physical activity in patients with MFS based on aortic diameter, family history of aortic dissection, and pre-existing fitness.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for imaging follow-up in Loeys–Dietz syndrome

rows.recommendation: In patients with Loeys–Dietz syndrome, TTE at baseline and subsequently every 6–12 months, depending on aortic diameter and growth, is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for imaging and surgery in ACTA2-related heritable thoracic aortic disease

rows.recommendation: Annual monitoring of the aortic root/ascending aorta with TTE to evaluate for aortic root/ascending aorta enlargement is recommended.
Imaging of the aorta with CMR/CCT every 3–5 years is recommended.
Prophylactic aortic root surgery should be considered with a diameter ≥45 mm, or lower in cases with other risk factors.

content.title: 5.3. Vascular examination of peripheral arteries
content.narrative_summary: This section describes the ankle–brachial index (ABI) as a low-cost, easy tool for PAD diagnosis and surveillance, usable at rest or after exercise. Both oscillometric and Doppler methods show good concordance. Resting ABI has 68–84% sensitivity and 84–99% specificity for PAD; an ABI ≤0.90 confirms disease. For values >1.40 (seen in arterial stiffness due to diabetes, kidney failure, or age), non-compressible arteries are indicated. Toe–brachial index (TBI) is recommended when ABI >1.40. Toe pressure assesses medium-calibre artery rigidity, with Doppler or plethysmography methods providing PAD sensitivity and specificity.

section_headings: 5.3.2 Digital subtraction angiography, computed tomography angiography, and magnetic resonance angiography
content.narrative_summary: This page continues the discussion of diagnostic modalities for peripheral arterial disease. Duplex ultrasound (DUS) is described as a dynamic, non-invasive, radiation- and contrast-free examination that localizes vascular lesions, quantifies severity via velocity criteria, and assesses hemodynamic relevance; it has 88% sensitivity and 95% specificity for >50% stenosis, with post-exercise DUS and contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) as adjuncts. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) remains primarily for revascularization procedures; computed tomography angiography (CTA) offers superior spatial resolution but may overestimate stenosis due to blooming, while magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) allows vessel wall and perfusion assessment. The aorta is divided into anatomical regions for reporting, and aortic diameters should be measured in echocardiography using the leading-to-leading edge method (≈2 mm systolic expansion) in all segments; inner-to-inner edge measurements are used in CT/CMR, and outer-to-outer diameters are recommended when wall thickening or aortic dissection is present.

section_headings: 5.4.5 Duplex ultrasound imaging of the abdominal aorta
content.narrative_summary: The page discusses the role of transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE) in aortic disease, noting its high sensitivity (up to 99%) and specificity (89% for AAS), utility at the bedside and intraoperatively, limitations for long-term surveillance requiring CCT/CMR, and recommendations by major professional societies amid ongoing methodological debate. It then details duplex ultrasound imaging of the abdominal aorta, emphasizing measurement of the anteroposterior diameter in transverse and longitudinal views, beam perpendicularity, and the outer-to-outer and mean ellipse diameter methods. Subsequent sections introduce cardiovascular computed tomography protocols for aortic assessment, cardiovascular magnetic resonance techniques and their advantages and limitations, and begin a discussion of positron emission tomography.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 4 — Recommendations for thoracic aortic measurements

rows.recommendation: TTE is recommended as the first-line imaging technique in evaluating thoracic aortic diseases.
It is recommended to report aortic diameters using the leading-to-leading edge convention in end-diastole by echocardiography.
It is recommended to report aortic diameters using the inner-to-inner edge convention in end-diastole by CCT or CMR.
It is recommended to report aortic diameters from images obtained with the double-oblique technique (not axial images) by CCT or CMR.
ECG-triggered CCT is recommended for comprehensive diagnosis, follow-up, and pre-invasive treatment assessment of the entire aorta, particularly the root and ascending aorta.
CMR is recommended for diagnosis and follow-up of thoracic aortic diseases, especially when chronic follow-up is required.
The aortic root should be measured using the cusp-to-cusp distance. Also, the presence of asymmetry (>5 mm) among distances should be reported.

content.narrative_summary: Ankle–brachial index (ABI) is recommended as the initial non-invasive test to confirm lower-limb decreased perfusion, with an ABI ≤0.90 diagnostic of PAD. In cases of ABI >0.90 and clinical suspicion, post-exercise ABI or imaging (preferably treadmill) should be considered; a post-exercise ABI decrease >20% may serve as a diagnostic criterion. For abnormally high ABI values (>1.4) or in patients with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia and diabetes, toe pressure (TP), toe-brachial index (TBI), transcutaneous oxygen pressure (TcPO2), pulse volume recordings, and distal Doppler waveform analysis should be used, with ABI estimable from distal Doppler independent of diabetes and medial sclerosis. content.narrative_summary: Patients with peripheral arterial disease (PAD) should receive comprehensive optimal medical therapy (OMT), including supervised exercise training and lifestyle modification, along with personalized pharmacotherapy to reduce major adverse cardiovascular (MACE) and limb events (MALE). PAD patients are less likely to receive OMT than those with coronary artery disease. Exercise therapy encompasses supervised exercise training (SET) with medical screening, treadmill protocols, and measurement of pain-free and maximal walking distance, health-related quality of life, and cardiorespiratory fitness. Home-based exercise training (HBET) is an alternative when SET is unavailable, though less effective. SET should be conducted at least three times per week for 30–60 minutes over a minimum of 12 weeks, with exercise to moderate-severe claudication pain to improve walking performance. A flexible, patient-centered approach to pain tolerance is recommended.

content.narrative_summary: The section discusses antithrombotic therapy in patients with PAD. In asymptomatic PAD, trials of antiplatelet agents (aspirin) did not show benefits on MACE or revascularization, though subgroup effects cannot be excluded. In symptomatic PAD, antithrombotic therapy improves prognosis: clopidogrel may modestly outperform aspirin; ticagrelor showed no superiority in EUCLID. Dual therapy with aspirin and vascular-dose rivaroxaban reduces MACE, MALE, and acute limb ischaemia but increases major bleeding. Post-endovascular DAPT for 1–3 months improves patency without increasing mortality. Vitamin K antagonists may be considered for selected high-risk conduits. In patients requiring OAC for other indications, anticoagulation is warranted and SAPT post-endovascular therapy should be brief.

content.narrative_summary:
Under medical treatment (Section 8.1.2.2), management of chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI) must include optimal medical therapy: pain relief, rest, wound care, infection control, and involvement of a multidisciplinary vascular team to prevent amputation. Lower-limb exercise is contraindicated until ulcers heal, and aggressive offloading should be ensured. Oral antibiotics may suffice depending on infection, but systemic signs require intravenous therapy. Various dressings (antimicrobial, silver, collagen, honey/iodine, platelet-rich plasma, negative pressure) may accelerate healing. content.title: 8.3.2 Renal artery disease
content.narrative_summary: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis (RAS) accounts for over 90% of RAS cases, with varying prevalence by age and sex. Clinical presentation includes renovascular hypertension, impaired renal function, and flash pulmonary oedema. Diagnosis relies on non-invasive imaging (duplex ultrasonography, contrast-enhanced MRA, CT angiography) with thresholds for PSV and resistance index, with catheter angiography as the gold standard. Prognosis correlates with stenosis severity and predicts mortality. Treatment strategies include medical therapy—antithrombotic agents in atherosclerotic RAS—and revascularization, where endovascular stenting and open surgery have roles depending on patient anatomy, with mixed evidence on benefit.

content.narrative_summary: Thoracic aortic aneurysm patients are usually asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally, with possible chest pain, aortic regurgitation, and compression symptoms. Those with root involvement (e.g., HTAD) have higher risk of acute aortic events. Degenerative TAAs grow faster in women and carry a threefold higher risk of events; at 57.5 mm diameter, yearly rupture, dissection, and death rates are 3.6%, 3.7%, and 10.8%, respectively. Descending thoracic and thoracoabdominal aneurysms can extend into the abdominal aorta; TAAAs are classified into five groups (see Figure 22) to guide risk stratification and surgical planning. Most are degenerative with calcification, though trauma, infection, inflammation, or genetic factors may contribute.

content.narrative_summary: Section 9.2.2.4 discusses surveillance of thoracic aortic aneurysms (TAA), emphasizing chronic follow-up with clinical evaluation and imaging tailored to aneurysm location: TTE, CCT, or CMR for root/ascending aorta; CMR/CCT preferred when involving arch/DTA; CMR over CCT to minimize radiation when stable. Section 9.2.3 defines abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) as dilation ≥1.5× normal (≥30 mm), usually fusiform, lined with thrombus, prevalence rising with age and male predominance. AAAs classified by relation to renal arteries; risk factors include smoking, male sex, family history, diabetes (lower risk), inflammation, genetic disorders; mean growth ~3 mm/year. Two-thirds asymptomatic; rupture risk dependent on size, higher in women. Surveillance of AAAs: low risk if <25 mm, re-assessment intervals based on diameter, DUS standard, CCT for detailed visualization, CMR for radiation-sensitive patients.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of surveillance intervals for abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), reporting that meta-analyses recommend varied follow-up intervals by aneurysm size and sex, with an algorithm in Figure 24 and shorter intervals for rapid growth (≥10 mm/year or ≥5 mm in 6 months). content.narrative_summary: The text discusses recommendations for interventional treatment of acute Type A aortic dissection (TAAD), stating that immediate surgical repair is recommended despite high perioperative mortality (17%–25%) and neurological complication rates (18%). Registry data (IRAD and GERAADA) show lower mortality with surgery versus medical management. Advances in surgical and anesthetic techniques have improved post-operative survival. Long-term follow-up favors surgical intervention even in challenging cases. Predictors of post-operative mortality include cardiogenic shock secondary to tamponade, malperfusion syndromes, and advanced age; in-hospital mortality in octogenarians was lower with surgery than with conservative treatment, although some studies report non-significant differences due to small sample sizes. Quality-of-life outcomes in elderly patients are mixed.

rows.recommendation: In patients with AAS, immediate anti-impulse treatment targeting SBP <120 mmHg and heart rate ≤60 b.p.m. is recommended. In cases of spinal ischaemia or concomitant brain injury, maintaining higher MAP is recommended.
Intravenous BBs (e.g. labetalol or esmolol) are recommended as first-line agents. If necessary, i.v. vasodilators (e.g. dihydropyridine calcium blockers or nitrates) could be added.
Invasive monitoring with an arterial line and continuous three-lead ECG recording, as well as admission to an intensive care unit, is recommended.

In patients with AAS who can be managed conservatively and who achieved haemodynamic targets with i.v. anti-impulse therapy, switching to oral BBs and, if necessary, up-titration of other BP-lowering agents, is recommended after 24 h if gastrointestinal transit is preserved.
Adequate pain control to achieve haemodynamic targets is recommended.
If the patient has a contraindication for BBs, a non-dihydropyridine calcium blocker should be considered.

content.narrative_summary: The text discusses management strategies for malperfusion in aortic dissection and the evolving role of endovascular therapy in type B aortic dissection (TBAD). It notes that endovascular therapy is now first-line for complicated acute TBAD when anatomy is favorable, with open surgery reserved for unsuitable cases. Trials (ADSORB, INSTEAD-XL) suggest early intervention in uncomplicated and subacute TBAD may improve outcomes, and prophylactic TEVAR could reduce late aortic-related events in high-risk patients. The ongoing IMPROVE-AD trial will compare upfront TEVAR plus medical therapy versus medical therapy with surveillance. The DISSECT classification system (Duration, Intimal tear, Size, Segmental extent, Clinical complications, Thrombosis) is introduced to guide treatment decisions. A meta-analysis showed TEVAR is superior to best medical therapy in uncomplicated acute TBAD, providing similar early outcomes, fewer long-term events, and better aortic remodeling. Accurate endograft sizing using imaging modalities (CT, IVUS, TOE, 3D CCT) is emphasized, and further research is needed on intraoperative imaging and long-term outcomes.

section_headings: 9.3.1.4.4. Chronic type B aortic dissection interventional treatment
content.narrative_summary: Chronic TBAD is defined as dissection ≥3 months after symptom onset, including residual dissection after TAAD repair. Aortic complications, especially aneurysmal degeneration, occur in up to 50%. Indications for intervention include new aortic symptoms (rapid expansion, malperfusion, rupture). Asymptomatic aneurysmal dilation is the main risk factor for rupture, rising when diameter exceeds 55 mm; reported rupture risk is 15.3%–18.8% for diameters between 50–55 mm. Open repair remains first-line for low-risk or HTAD patients, with surgical mortality 6%–11% and spinal cord ischaemia rates 3%–11%, supporting centralisation in experienced centres. TEVAR offers high technical success (∼90%) and false lumen thrombosis (∼86%) but often requires lifelong surveillance and may need fenestrated/branched endografts for distal seal. Management during pregnancy requires multidisciplinary care using lowest‐teratogenic drugs, with caesarean delivery timed by foetal viability.

content.narrative_summary: Intramural haematoma (IMH) involves vasa vasorum haemorrhage within the aortic media in 5–25% of acute aortic syndrome cases, most often affecting the descending thoracic aorta. Diagnosis relies on imaging, notably nonenhanced and contrast-enhanced CCT and CMR demonstrating crescentic or circular wall thickening, while TTE has low sensitivity. Clinical outcomes include progression to aortic dissection (12%), aneurysm formation or intramural dissection, with partial or total regression in about one-third of patients. In‐hospital mortality is approximately 26.6% for type A IMH and 4.4% for type B IMH in surgical cohorts. Geographic variation shows higher early detection and lower mortality in Eastern centers. Management parallels acute aortic dissection: urgent surgery for type A IMH, with a possible watch-and-wait approach for uncomplicated cases; medical management and imaging surveillance for uncomplicated type B, with endovascular or surgical interventions reserved for high-risk or complicated presentations.

content.narrative_summary: In the absence of clinical trials, a shared‐decision model is used for Turner syndrome medical treatment: consider beta‐blockers and angiotensin receptor blockers to inhibit aortic growth and treat hypertension per general guidelines; hormonal therapies (growth hormone in childhood; oestrogen/progesterone and thyroid hormones) require multidisciplinary team discussion. Aortic aneurysm surgery in Turner syndrome should be individualized, accounting for bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation, uncontrolled hypertension (despite >3 antihypertensive drugs), rapid aortic growth (≥3 mm/year), and planned pregnancy. Turner syndrome pregnancies elevate risk of aortic dissection; prophylactic surgery is recommended when ASI ≥25 mm/m2, based on expert shared‐decision processes. Physical exercise benefits cardiovascular risk and quality of life, and structural defects with aortic diameters should guide sports participation recommendations.

content.narrative_summary: This page details vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (vEDS), an autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic COL3A1 variants leading to type III collagen dysfunction, with major complications including arterial dissections, aneurysms, and rupture. Prognosis varies by variant type, with null variants having better outcomes; recurrence risk is 1.6 events per 5 years and life expectancy averages around 51 years. Surveillance through DUS, CCT, or CMR is recommended. Medical management is based on blood pressure control, notably using celiprolol, while surgical interventions for arterial complications require urgent imaging and cautious, case-by-case decisions. Pregnancy in vEDS carries risks of arterial and uterine complications and requires shared decision-making. The page also introduces Marfan syndrome, caused by FBN1 variants, characterized by aortic root aneurysm and dissection, multisystem involvement, and the importance of genetic testing and imaging surveillance (echocardiography, CMR/CCT, DUS).

section_headings: 10.2. Aortic disease associated with bicuspid aortic valves
content.narrative_summary: This section introduces bicuspid aortic valves (BAV) as the most common congenital heart defect (0.5%–2% of live births) and a distinct risk factor for aortic valve disease associated with heterogeneous valvulo-aortopathy. The inheritance pattern is predominantly autosomal dominant in some families, but no single-gene model explains most cases. Multiple genes implicated in embryogenesis and cell differentiation have each been associated with BAV-related aortopathy in fewer than 5% of cases.

Surgery for bicuspid aortopathy of the root phenotype is recommended when the maximum aortic diameter is ≥50 mm.

Screening by TTE in FDRs of BAV patients with root phenotype aortopathy and/or isolated aortic regurgitation is recommended.

Surveillance serial imaging by TTE is recommended in BAV patients with a maximum aortic diameter >40 mm, either with no indication for surgery or after isolated aortic valve surgery, after 1 year, then if stability is observed, every 2–3 years.
Screening by TTE in FDRs of all BAV patients should be considered.
In patients with low surgical risk, surgery for bicuspid aortopathy of ascending phenotype should be considered when the maximum aortic diameter is >52 mm.

section_headings: 10.3. Coarctation of the aorta and aortic arch variants
content.narrative_summary: This section describes the definition and epidemiology of coarctation of the aorta (CoA), associated lesions (e.g., BAV, aneurysms), and its occurrence in syndromes such as Turner syndrome. It outlines the diagnostic work-up in adults, including the importance of blood pressure gradients, imaging modalities, and the lack of evidence for intracerebral aneurysm screening in asymptomatic patients. The treatment and follow-up subsection emphasizes first-line stenting or surgical graft interposition for native or re-coarctation, lifelong follow-up with CCT/CMR every 3–5 years, hypertension management, and indications for endovascular intervention based on anatomical narrowing and pressure gradients.

rows.recommendation: In patients with low surgical risk and ascending phenotype bicuspid aortopathy, surgery should be considered at a maximum diameter ≥50 mm if any of the following is the case: Age <50 years; Shorter stature; Ascending aortic length ≥11 cm; Aortic diameter growth rate ≥3 mm per year; Family history of acute aortic syndrome; Aortic coarctation; Resistant hypertension; Concomitant non-aortic-valve cardiac surgery; Desire for pregnancy.
Surgery for bicuspid aortopathy in patients undergoing aortic valve surgery should be considered at a root or ascending diameter ≥45 mm.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation Table 69 — Recommendations for evaluation and medical treatment of patients with coarctation of the aorta

rows.recommendation: In patients with native or repaired coarctation, lifelong follow-up is recommended, including regular imaging of the aorta with CCT/CMR every 3–5 years (adapted to clinical status and previous imaging findings).

Coarctation or re-coarctation repair (either surgical or endovascular) is indicated in patients with hypertension with an increased non-invasive gradient between the upper and lower limbs (decreased ABI) confirmed with invasive measurement (peak-to-peak >20 mmHg), with a preference for stenting when technically feasible.
In patients with coarctation, BP measurements at both arms and one lower extremity are recommended.
It is recommended to treat hypertension in patients with coarctation according to ESC hypertension guidelines.

Endovascular treatment should be considered in patients with hypertension with >50% narrowing relative to the aortic diameter at the diaphragm, even if the invasive peak-to-peak gradient is <20 mmHg, when technically feasible.
Endovascular treatment should be considered in normotensive patients with an increased non-invasive gradient confirmed with invasive peak-to-peak gradient >20 mmHg, when technically feasible.

content.narrative_summary: The page continues discussion of aortic disease management, noting that atherosclerotic upper extremity arterial disease (UAED) often affects the subclavian artery and that duplex ultrasound (DUS) is first-line imaging; acute superior mesenteric artery (SMA) occlusion requires immediate revascularization. Hybrid approaches and advanced endovascular therapies are increasingly used, and acute aortic syndrome management involves critical care treatment and selective surgery. Genetic aortic conditions warrant evaluation of patients and first-degree relatives (FDRs) with family history and syndromic features, and comprehensive vascular assessment with personalized surveillance thresholds. Section 13 lists gaps in evidence for peripheral arterial disease research priorities across eight areas including epidemiology, biomarkers, peripheral artery evaluation, screening, OMT, aneurysm risk stratification, acute syndromes, genetic aortic diseases, and sex differences. rows.recommendation: When managing PAAD, it is recommended to adopt a comprehensive approach that addresses the entirety of arterial circulation.
To assess PAAD, it is recommended to perform thorough clinical, vascular, and CVRF laboratory evaluation.
Measurement of the ABI is recommended as the first-line non-invasive test for screening and diagnosis of PAD, using an ABI ≤0.90 as a diagnostic criterion.
In the case of non-compressible ankle arteries or ABI >1.40, additional methods such as TP, TBI or Doppler waveform analysis are recommended.
It is recommended that aortic diameters are measured at prespecified anatomical landmarks, and the largest diameter of the section be perpendicular to the longitudinal axis.
It is recommended in cases of serial imaging of the aorta over time to use the same imaging modality with the same measurement method.

It is recommended to consider renal function, pregnancy, age, and history of allergy to contrast media to select the optimal imaging modality with minimal radiation exposure and lowest iatrogenic risk, except for emergency cases.
TTE is recommended as the first-line imaging technique in evaluating thoracic aortic diseases.
It is recommended to report aortic diameters using the leading-to-leading edge convention in end-diastole by echocardiography.
It is recommended to report aortic diameters using the inner-to-inner edge convention in end-diastole by CCT or CMR.
It is recommended to report aortic diameters from images obtained with the double-oblique technique (not axial images) by CCT or CMR.
ECG-triggered CCT is recommended for comprehensive diagnosis, follow-up, and pre-invasive treatment assessment of the entire aorta, particularly the root and ascending aorta.
CMR is recommended for diagnosis and follow-up of thoracic aortic diseases, especially when chronic follow-up is required.
Screening is recommended in men aged ≥65 years and with a history of smoking to reduce the risk of death from ruptured AAA.
Screening is recommended in FDRs of patients with AAA aged ≥50, unless an acquired cause can be clearly identified.
In patients with PAAD, cessation and abstinence from smoking of any kind is recommended to reduce the risk of AD, MI, death, and limb ischaemia.
A healthy diet rich in legumes, dietary fibre, nuts, fruits, and vegetables, with a high flavonoid intake (Mediterranean diet), is recommended for CV disease prevention in patients with PAAD.
Low- to moderate-intensity (or high if tolerated) aerobic activities are recommended in patients with PAD to increase overall and pain-free walking distance.
In patients with PAAD, behavioural counselling to promote healthy diet, smoking cessation, and physical activity is recommended to improve the CV risk profile.
It is recommended to promote patient and caregivers’ education and empowerment through tailored guidance on lifestyle adjustments and the importance of regular physical activity.
In patients with PAAD and hypertension an SBP target towards 120–129 mmHg, if tolerated, is recommended.
In unilateral RAS patients, it is recommended that antihypertensive medication include ACEIs/ARBs.
In patients with atherosclerotic PAAD, lipid-lowering therapy is recommended.
An ultimate LDL-C goal of <1.4 mmol/L (55 mg/dL) and a >50% reduction in LDL-C vs. baseline are recommended in patients with atherosclerotic PAAD.
Statins are recommended in all patients with PAD.
If the target LDL-C level is not achieved, a combination of statins and ezetimibe is indicated in patients with atherosclerotic PAAD, to achieve the given target values.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of patients presenting with acute limb ischaemia

rows.recommendation: In patients with ALI, it is recommended that an urgent evaluation is performed by a vascular clinician with sufficient experience to assess limb viability and implement appropriate therapy.

In cases of neurological deficit, urgent revascularization is recommended; diagnostic imaging is recommended to guide treatment, provided it does not delay treatment, or if the need for primary amputation is obvious.
In the absence of severe neurological deficit, revascularization is recommended within hours of initial imaging in a case-by-case decision.
Treatment with analgesics is recommended as soon as possible for pain control.
It is recommended to monitor for compartment syndrome after revascularization and treat (fasciotomy).
It is recommended to assess clinical and haemodynamic success following revascularization.
In patients with ALI, it is recommended to obtain a comprehensive medical history and determine the cause of thrombosis and/or embolization.

It is not recommended to use the ECST method for ICA stenosis assessment.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for antithrombotic treatment in patients with carotid stenosis

rows.recommendation: In patients with symptomatic CS, not undergoing carotid endarterectomy or stenting, DAPT with low-dose aspirin and clopidogrel (75 mg) is recommended for the first 21 days or longer, followed by clopidogrel 75 mg or long-term aspirin to reduce the risk of stroke.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for interventional treatment in patients with asymptomatic carotid artery stenosis

rows.recommendation: In asymptomatic patients with ICA stenosis, in the absence of high-risk features and with a life expectancy <5 years, routine revascularization is not recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for evaluation and medical treatment in patients with symptomatic carotid artery stenosis

rows.recommendation: DAPT is recommended in the early phase of minor strokes in patients with ICA stenosis, if not revascularized, for at least 21 days, considering the bleeding risk.

If indicated, it is recommended to perform CEA within 14 days in symptomatic ICA stenosis patients.
OMT is recommended for all symptomatic ICA stenosis patients.
Revascularization is not recommended in patients with ICA lesions <50%.

After ICA stent implantation, DAPT with aspirin and clopidogrel is recommended for at least 1 month.
After ICA revascularization, long-term aspirin or clopidogrel is recommended.
During follow-up, it is recommended to assess neurological symptoms, CVRFs, and treatment adherence at least yearly in patients with CS.
After ICA revascularization, surveillance with DUS is recommended within the first month.

In thoracic aortic dilatation, CCT or CMR is recommended to confirm TTE measurements, rule out aortic asymmetry, and determine baseline diameters for follow-up.
TTE is not recommended for the surveillance of aneurysms in the distal ascending aorta, aortic arch, or DTA.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for surveillance of patients with abdominal aortic aneurysm

rows.recommendation: DUS surveillance is recommended every 6 months in men with AAA of 50–55 mm and in women with AAA of 45–50 mm.
DUS is recommended for AAA surveillance.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for medical treatment in patients with thoracic aorta or abdominal aortic aneurysms

rows.recommendation: In patients with aortic aneurysm (TAA and/or AAA), optimal implementation of CV risk management and medical treatment (see detailed recommendations in dedicated Tables of Recommendations) are recommended to reduce MACE.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for surgery in aortic root and ascending aorta dilatation associated with tricuspid aortic valve

VKAs are recommended lifelong for all patients with a Bentall procedure with an MHV prosthesis.

rows.recommendation: In patients with low or intermediate operative risk with an aortic arch aneurysm and recurrent episodes of chest pain not attributable to non-aortic causes, open surgical replacement of the arch is recommended.

content.narrative_summary: This page presents a series of structured recommendation tables covering: management of descending thoracic and thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysms; management of abdominal aortic aneurysm; management of endoleaks; follow-up after aortic aneurysm treatment; diagnostic work-up of acute aortic syndrome; and medical treatment in acute aortic syndromes.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of patients presenting with descending thoracic aortic and thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysms

rows.recommendation: In patients with unruptured DTA aneurysm (without HTAD), elective repair is recommended if diameter ≥55 mm.
In patients without HTAD with unruptured DTA aneurysm, when elective repair is indicated and anatomy is suitable, TEVAR is recommended over open repair.
In patients with DTA aneurysm who undergo TEVAR with planned LSA coverage, it is recommended to revascularize the LSA before TEVAR to reduce the risk of SCI and stroke.
In patients with unruptured degenerative TAAA, elective repair is recommended when the diameter is ≥60 mm.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of patients presenting with abdominal aortic aneurysm

rows.recommendation: Elective repair is recommended if AAA diameter is ≥55 mm in men or ≥50 mm in women.
In ruptured AAA with suitable anatomy, endovascular repair is recommended over open repair to reduce peri-operative morbidity and mortality.
In patients with AAA and limited life expectancy (<2 years), elective AAA repair is not recommended.
Prior to AAA repair, routine evaluation with coronary angiography and systematic revascularization in patients with chronic coronary syndromes is not recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of patients presenting with endoleaks

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to perform 30 day imaging after TEVAR/EVAR, by CCT + DUS/CEUS, to assess the success of intervention.
It is recommended to re-intervene to achieve a seal in patients with type I endoleak after TEVAR/EVAR.
It is recommended to re-intervene, principally by endovascular means, to achieve a seal in patients with type III endoleak after TEVAR/EVAR.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for follow-up after treatment of aortic aneurysms

rows.recommendation: After open repair of TAA, early CCT is recommended within 1 month, and then yearly CCT follow-up for the first 2 post-operative years and every 5 years thereafter if findings are stable.
After TEVAR, follow-up imaging is recommended at 1 and 12 months post-operatively, then yearly until the fifth post-operative year if no abnormalities are documented.
After open repair of AAA, first follow-up imaging is recommended within 1 post-operative year, and then every 5 years thereafter if findings are stable.

After EVAR, follow-up imaging is recommended with CCT (or CMR) and DUS/CEUS at 1 month and 12 months post-operatively, then, if no abnormalities are documented, DUS/CEUS is recommended every year, repeating CCT or CMR (based on potential artefacts) every 5 years.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for diagnostic work-up of acute aortic syndrome

rows.recommendation: In unstable patients who cannot be transferred to CCT, TOE is recommended for diagnosis and evaluation of the coeliac trunk and mesenteric artery.
In patients presenting with clinical features compatible with possible AAS, a multiparametric algorithm for ruling in or out AAS using the ADD-RS is recommended.

ECG-gated CCT from neck to pelvis is recommended as the first-line imaging technique in patients with a suspected AAS since it is widely available, accurate, and provides information about the entry tear, extension, and possible complications (malperfusion, dilatation, or rupture).
In patients with suspected AAS, focused TTE (with use of contrast if feasible) is recommended during the initial evaluation.
In patients with suspected AAS, TOE is recommended to guide peri-operative management and detect complications.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendation for medical treatment in acute aortic syndromes

rows.recommendation: In patients with AAS, immediate anti-impulse treatment targeting SBP <120 mmHg and heart rate ≤60 b.p.m. is recommended. In cases of spinal ischaemia or concomitant brain injury, maintaining higher MAP is recommended.
Intravenous BBs (e.g. labetalol) are recommended as first-line agents. If necessary, i.v. vasodilators (e.g. dihydropyridine calcium blockers or nitrates) could be added.
Invasive monitoring with an arterial line and continuous three-lead ECG recording, as well as admission to an intensive care unit, is recommended.

In patients with AAS who can be managed conservatively and who achieved haemodynamic targets with i.v. anti-impulse therapy, switching to oral BBs and, if necessary, up-titration of other BP-lowering agents, is recommended after 24 h if gastrointestinal transit is preserved.
Adequate pain control to achieve haemodynamic targets is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for intervention in type A acute aortic dissection

rows.recommendation: In patients with acute TAAD, emergency surgical consultation and evaluation and immediate surgical intervention is recommended.

In patients with acute TAAD who have extensive destruction of the aortic root, a root aneurysm, or a known genetic aortic disorder, aortic root replacement is recommended with a mechanical or biological valved conduit.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for aortic repair strategies in type A acute aortic dissection

rows.recommendation: In patients with acute TAAD and a partially dissected aortic root but no significant aortic valve leaflet pathology, aortic valve resuspension is recommended over valve replacement.
In patients with acute TAAD undergoing aortic repair, an open distal anastomosis is recommended to improve survival and increase FL thrombosis rates.
In patients with acute TAAD without an intimal tear in the arch or a significant arch aneurysm, hemi-arch repair is recommended over more extensive arch replacement.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of malperfusion in the setting of acute aortic dissection

rows.recommendation: In patients with acute TAAD presenting with malperfusion (cerebral, mesenteric, lower limb, or renal), immediate aortic surgery is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of patients presenting with acute type B aortic dissection

rows.recommendation: Medical therapy including pain relief and blood pressure control is recommended in all patients with acute TBAD.
In patients with complicated acute TBAD, emergency intervention is recommended.
In patients with complicated acute TBAD, TEVAR is recommended as the first-line therapy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of patients presenting with chronic type B aortic dissection

rows.recommendation: Antihypertensive therapy is recommended in all patients with chronic TBAD.
In chronic TBAD with acute symptoms of malperfusion, rupture, or progression of disease, emergency intervention is recommended.
In patients with chronic TBAD and a descending thoracic aortic diameter ≥60 mm, treatment is recommended in patients at reasonable surgical risk.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of intramural haematoma

rows.recommendation: In patients with IMH, medical therapy including pain relief and blood pressure control is recommended.
In type A IMH, urgent surgery is recommended.
In type B IMH, initial medical therapy under careful surveillance is recommended.
In uncomplicated type B IMH, repetitive imaging (CCT or CMR) is indicated.
In complicated type B IMH, TEVAR is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer

rows.recommendation: In all patients with PAU, medical therapy including pain relief and blood pressure control is recommended.
In cases of type A PAU, surgery is recommended.
In cases of type B PAU, initial medical therapy under careful surveillance is recommended.
In uncomplicated type B PAU, repetitive imaging (CMR, CCT, or TOE) is recommended.
In complicated type B PAU, endovascular treatment (TEVAR) is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for traumatic aortic injury

rows.recommendation: In cases of severe aortic injury (grade 4), immediate repair is recommended.
In cases of TAI with suitable anatomy requiring intervention, TEVAR is recommended over open surgery.
In all TAI patients, medical therapy including pain relief, and blood pressure and heart rate control, is recommended.
In cases of TAI suspicion, CCT is recommended.
In cases of moderate aortic injury (grade 3), repair is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for follow-up after treatment of acute aortic syndrome

rows.recommendation: After TEVAR for AAS, follow-up imaging is recommended at 1, 6, and 12 months post-operatively, then yearly until the fifth post-operative year if no abnormalities are documented.
In medically treated type B AAD or IMH, follow-up imaging is recommended at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months after onset, then yearly if imaging findings are stable.
In medically treated PAU, follow-up imaging is recommended at 1 month after diagnosis, then every 6 months if imaging findings are stable.

content.narrative_summary: This page presents structured recommendation tables covering the management, genetic testing, imaging, medical treatment, surgical intervention, pregnancy care, and physical exercise guidance for patients with heritable thoracic aortic disease, Turner syndrome, vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, and Marfan syndrome.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for the management of patients with heritable thoracic aortic disease

rows.recommendation: It is recommended that medical management of patients with HTAD is individualized and based on shared decision-making.
It is recommended that patients with known or suspected syndromic or non-syndromic HTAD are evaluated in a centre with experience in the care of this patient group.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for genetic testing and aortic screening in aortic disease

rows.recommendation: In patients with aortic root/ascending aneurysms or thoracic aortic dissection, gathering family history information for at least three generations about TAD, unexplained sudden deaths, and peripheral and intracranial aneurysms is recommended.

In patients with aortic root/ascending aortic aneurysms or thoracic aortic dissection and risk factors for HTAD, genetic counselling at an expert centre and subsequent testing, if indicated, is recommended.
In patients with HTAD who have a pathogenic/likely pathogenic variant, genetic testing of at-risk biological relatives (i.e. cascade testing) is recommended, irrespective of age.
In patients with TAD with risk factors for HTAD, with a negative family history of TAD and in whom no (likely) pathogenic variant is identified, TTE screening aortic imaging of FDRs is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for imaging in women with Turner syndrome

rows.recommendation: To take the smaller body size of women (≥15 years) with TS into account, the use of the ascending ASI (ratio of aortic diameter [mm] to BSA [m²]), AHI (ratio of aortic diameter [mm] to height [m]), or aortic z-score is recommended to define the degree of aortic dilatation and assess the risk of aortic dissection.
It is recommended to define imaging and clinical surveillance intervals according to the estimated risk for dissection, based on the ascending ASI and concomitant lesions.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for medical treatment in patients with vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome

rows.recommendation: In patients with vEDS, regular vascular surveillance of the aorta and peripheral arteries by DUS, CCT, or CMR is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for vascular imaging in Marfan syndrome

rows.recommendation:
In patients with MFS, TTE is recommended:
• At least annually in patients with an aortic root diameter <45 mm in the absence of additional risk factors
• At least every 6 months in patients with an aortic root diameter <45 mm in the presence of additional risk factors
• At least every 6–12 months in patients with an aortic root diameter ≥45 mm in the absence of additional risk factors

In patients without previous aortic surgery, complete peripheral vascular and thoracoabdominal aorta imaging by CMR or CCT and DUS is recommended at the first evaluation, and subsequently every 3–5 years if stable.
In patients with MFS who have undergone aortic root replacement, surveillance imaging of the thoracic aorta by CMR (or CCT) is recommended at least every 3 years.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for medical treatment in Marfan syndrome

rows.recommendation: In patients with MFS, treatment with either a BB or an ARB, in maximally tolerated doses (unless contraindicated), is recommended to reduce the rate of aortic dilatation.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for aortic surgery in Marfan syndrome

rows.recommendation: Surgery is indicated in patients with MFS who have aortic root disease with a maximal aortic sinus diameter ≥50 mm.

Surgery to replace the aortic root and ascending aorta, using the valve-sparing surgery technique, is recommended in patients with MFS or related HTAD with aortic root dilatation when anatomical features of the valve allow its preservation and the surgeon has specific expertise.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for pregnancy in women with Marfan syndrome

rows.recommendation: Have a pre-conception evaluation to address the risks of maternal CV and other complications.
Have follow-up in a centre with access to a pregnancy heart and vessel team.
It is recommended that couples in which a partner has or is at risk of HTAD be offered pre-conception genetic counselling.
Imaging of the whole aorta (by CMR/CCT) is recommended prior to pregnancy.
Follow-up during pregnancy is recommended with a frequency determined by aortic diameter and growth.
Intake of BBs during pregnancy is recommended.
Prophylactic aortic root surgery is recommended in women desiring pregnancy with aortic diameters >45 mm.
ARBs are not recommended during pregnancy.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for physical exercise in patients with Marfan syndrome

rows.recommendation: It is recommended to individualize physical activity in patients with MFS based on aortic diameter, family history of aortic dissection, and pre-existing fitness.
Regular moderate aerobic exercise with a level of intensity informed by aortic diameter is recommended in most patients with MFS.

Below the recommendations, abbreviations are listed, followed by administrative sections on evidence tables, data availability, and the start of author information.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for imaging follow-up in Loeys–Dietz syndrome

rows.recommendation: In patients with Loeys–Dietz syndrome, TTE at baseline and subsequently every 6–12 months, depending on aortic diameter and growth, is recommended.
In patients with Loeys–Dietz syndrome, a baseline arterial imaging study from head to pelvis with CMR or CCT and subsequent surveillance with CMR or CCT or DUS every 1–3 years is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for imaging and surgery in ACTA2-related heritable thoracic aortic disease

rows.recommendation: Annual monitoring of the aortic root/ascending aorta with TTE to evaluate aortic root/ascending aorta enlargement is recommended.
Imaging of the aorta with CMR/CCT every 3–5 years is recommended.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for bicuspid aortic valve-associated aortopathy management

rows.recommendation: When a BAV is first diagnosed, initial TTE to assess diameters of the aorta at several levels is recommended.
Surgery for bicuspid aortopathy is recommended when the maximum aortic diameter is ≥55 mm.
Surgery for bicuspid aortopathy of the root phenotype is recommended when the maximum aortic diameter is ≥50 mm.

CCT or CMR of the entire thoracic aorta is recommended at first diagnosis and when important discrepancies in measurements are found between subsequent TTE controls during surveillance, or when the diameter of the aorta exceeds 45 mm.
Screening by TTE in FDRs of BAV patients with root phenotype aortopathy and/or isolated aortic regurgitation is recommended.

Surveillance serial imaging by TTE is recommended in BAV patients with a maximum aortic diameter >40 mm, either with no indication for surgery or after isolated aortic valve surgery, after 1 year, then if stability is observed, every 2–3 years.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for evaluation and medical treatment of patients with coarctation of the aorta

rows.recommendation: In patients with native or repaired coarctation, lifelong follow-up is recommended, including regular imaging of the aorta with CCT/CMR every 3–5 years (adapted to clinical status and previous imaging findings).

Coarctation or re-coarctation repair (either surgical or endovascular) is indicated in patients with hypertension with an increased non-invasive gradient between the upper and lower limbs (decreased ABI) confirmed with invasive measurement (peak-to-peak >20 mmHg), with a preference for stenting when technically feasible.
In patients with coarctation, BP measurements at both arms and one lower extremity are recommended.
It is recommended to treat hypertension in patients with coarctation according to ESC hypertension guidelines.

recommendation_tables.title: Recommendations for screening and management of polyvascular disease and peripheral arterial disease with cardiac diseases

rows.recommendation: In patients with PVD, an LDL-C reduction by ≥50% from baseline and an LDL-C goal of <1.4 mmol/L (<55 mg/dL) are recommended.
In patients with PAD and newly diagnosed AF with a CHA₂DS₂-VASc score ≥2, full oral anticoagulation is recommended.
Screening for ilio-femoral PAD is recommended in patients undergoing TAVI.
